title: Algebraic curves — function fields, divisors, and Riemann–Roch, Part II: global function-field arithmetic
summary: Arithmetic of a one-variable function field over its finite exact constant field: projective adeles and ideles, residue Fourier analysis, Artin–Schreier–Witt extensions, equal-characteristic class field theory, curve zeta functions and Schmidt’s theorem (degree-sensitive Chebotarev and Frobenius recognition are imported from DeligneWeightsAndPurity and ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations), reductive automorphic forms and the unitary Siegel–Eisenstein coefficients. Existing curve geometry, generic restricted products, local representation theory and Hermitian densities are imported. Certified arithmetic consumes finite-field factorization and point-count certificates.

nodes.title: Finite exact constants and the curve dictionary
nodes.statement: Let k be finite and K/k a one-variable function field. The finite relative algebraic closure k₀ of k in K is its unique exact constant field. With k₀ as base, the imported smooth projective curve is geometrically connected; its closed points identify with all normalized places of K/k₀. For any finite constant extension k₁/k₀, the compositum remains a field and the smooth curve base change has that function field. No rational point is assumed.
hypotheses: Finite k; explicit IsFunctionField k K. Geometric connectedness is asserted only after passing to the exact constants.
proofSteps: Use the pinned relative-constant-field theorem, then import AC.12’s normalization and anti-equivalence.
Apply AC.8’s constant-extension and place-splitting formulas. Purely inseparable field maps remain in AC.8 and do not become finite étale covers.

sources.match: Yu fixes a smooth projective geometrically connected curve over its full finite constant field. The normalization and exact-constant reduction are supplied by the native function-field declarations and AC.12, rather than proved in this introductory passage.

nodes.title: Divisor degree and Yu’s adelic degree
nodes.statement: For finite exact k=Fq and K=k(X), write d_v=[κ(v):k] and ord_v(π_v)=1. Divisor degree is Σ_v d_v D_v. The absolute value is |x|_v=q^(−d_v ord_v x). For an idele a, valuation degree deg_val(a)=Σ_v d_v ord_v(a_v), while Yu’s convention is deg_Yu(a)=−deg_val(a), so |a|=q^deg_Yu(a). For scalar aI_n in GL_n(A), determinant degree is n deg_Yu(a). In an unramified extension with arithmetic Artin normalization, a uniformizer maps to arithmetic Frobenius; geometric normalization takes the inverse.
hypotheses: Nonzero local entries; all sums finite on ideles; divisor degrees use the exact constants.
proofSteps: Import the weighted divisor degree and product formula. Apply them to the idele-divisor map in FA.2.
Keep the two signs as distinct homomorphisms; translate all GL_n and class-field formulas through this identity.

nodes.title: Divisor classes, Picard points and torsors
nodes.statement: For a smooth projective geometrically connected X/Fq with K=Fq(X), rational divisors modulo principal divisors identify with Pic(X), and the degree-zero subgroup identifies with Pic⁰_{X/Fq}(Fq). The comparison to rational points of the Picard scheme uses Br(Fq)=0; Pic¹ is a torsor, not a chosen point of X. A degree-one divisor selects an origin in Pic¹, while a rational point is stronger data. The finite group in the pinned class-number theorem is this degree-zero divisor class group, not the affine ideal class group attached to an omitted place.
hypotheses: Finite exact constants; full smooth projective curve; scheme Picard representability and Brauer descent imported.
proofSteps: Import SF.3/degree-zero-class-comparison (Cl⁰(F)≅Pic⁰(X)↪Pic⁰_{X/k}(k), cokernel inside Br(k)), AC.12’s divisor–line-bundle comparison and SF.3/picard-scheme-without-point and picard-brauer-sequence; no rational point is required.

nodes.title: Riemann–Roch basis certificates
nodes.statement: For finite exact k and a divisor D of K/k, an RR basis certificate is a finite family b:Fin r→K whose entries satisfy the native inequalities defining L(D), together with linear independence over k and equality of its k-span with the native riemannRochSpace D. The certificate verifies a computed basis, rather than replacing L(D). Its dimension is r, its coordinate map identifies L(D) with k^r, and equivalent divisors transport certificates by multiplication by the appropriate field unit.
hypotheses: Explicit function-field proof; exact constants; membership uses multiplicative valuations and includes zero.
proofSteps: Use the pinned finite-dimensionality theorem and native Basis to construct certificates.
Prove the coordinate and principal-transport API by restricted linear equivalences; computation requires the presentation and verifier in the next node.

nodes.title: Certified Riemann–Roch computation
nodes.statement: Input consists of a finite-field encoding, a separating presentation K=k(t)[y]/(f) with monic separable irreducible f, verified integral bases on finite and infinite charts, and a divisor represented by certified places. Construct a terminating algorithm returning an RR basis certificate. Reduce D’s valuation bounds to intersection of finitely generated fractional modules on the two charts, then compute their k-intersection by polynomial module reduction. Soundness, completeness and termination refer to these exact encodings; a finite list of functions satisfying the bounds alone is not a certificate of spanning.
hypotheses: All presentation and integral-basis data are verified; arbitrary singular plane coordinates do not constitute an integral basis. No complexity claim is made without the FA.7 cost model.
proofSteps: Import AC.2’s Dedekind chart and AC.6’s normalized place representation; factorization certificates come from FF.3.
Use Hess Proposition 9(iii) to identify L(D) with the intersection of the inverse finite and infinite divisor ideals. Choose verified module bases and their transition matrix over k(t).

Hess Lemma 1 gives the leading-coefficient noncancellation test. Each unimodular column reduction strictly decreases the sum of column degrees, bounded below by the determinant degree. Corollaries 3–4 diagonalize the two bases; Theorem 7 proves that the resulting t^j v_i with 0≤j≤d_i form the complete basis. Algorithm 13 returns those vectors and the transition-matrix certificate.

nodes.statement: For finite exact k and K/k, the diagonal image of K in A_K is discrete and cocompact. For each divisor D, A(D)={a:ord_v(a_v)≥−D_v for all v} is compact open. Its intersection with the diagonal is the native L(D), and the finite quotient A_K/(A(D)+K) agrees with the AC.4 repartition cokernel and has k-dimension equal to the index of specialty.

nodes.title: Completed residue functional
nodes.statement: For finite exact k and a nonzero rational differential ω, extend each native local component of its Weil differential uniquely to the completion K_v. On A_K the sum Res_ω(a)=Σ_v Res_v,ω(a_v) is finite: integral a_v at places where ω is regular contribute zero. It annihilates the diagonal by the global residue theorem.

proofSteps: Import AC.9’s residue comparison and AC.5’s interval-of-filtration quotient isomorphisms.
Factor the local functional through the relevant finite filtration quotient before completing. Sum only its finite nonzero support and import global residue vanishing.

It is a continuous unitary additive character, trivial on K; the pairing (a,b)↦ψ_ω(ab) identifies A_K with its Pontryagin dual and the annihilator of the diagonal K is exactly K. The local conductor exponent is n_v=ord_v(ω), in the convention triviality on π_v^(−n_v)O_v and failure on the next larger fractional ideal.

nodes.statement: For finite exact k, a nonzero ω and every locally constant compactly supported f:A_K→C, both sums over diagonal K are finite and Σ_{x∈K}f(x)=Σ_{x∈K}f̂(x), with the preceding character and measure. Translates of compact-open indicators are required to span the test-function space; unshifted A(D) indicators alone do not suffice.

nodes.title: Ramification import and inseparable boundary
nodes.statement: For finite separable L/K use AC.6–AC.8 for normalized valuations, integral closures, decomposition/inertia groups, different, discriminant and Riemann–Hurwitz. Import the lower/upper filtrations, Herbrand quotient and tower rules and Hasse–Arf from LocalFieldsRamification. Constant extensions are unramified and their local residue extensions have the specified constant Frobenius. Kummer covers require n prime to p and μ_n in the base. Purely inseparable Frobenius extensions are handled separately and never advertised as étale or with the separable different formula.
hypotheses: Finite extension with separability explicitly supplied in the ramification branch.
proofSteps: Apply the curve roadmap’s valuation restriction and local-to-global different comparisons.
Specialize the generic local filtration after completing at a chosen place; retain residue degree and constant extension data.

sources.match: Kosters–Wan uses ramification and conductors of finite ASW extensions. General different, separability, Hurwitz and upper/lower numbering are existing AC/LFR inputs; this node records their use rather than planning their general theory again.

acceptance: An unramified constant extension has trivial inertia.
The pth-power map of k(t) is purely inseparable and has no cyclic Galois interpretation.

nodes.title: Artin–Schreier–Witt quotient
nodes.statement: For any field F of characteristic p and n≥0, use native length-n p-typical Witt vectors with their Witt addition. Descend Witt Frobenius to W_n(F), define wp_n=Frob−id as an additive endomorphism, and form Q_n(F)=W_n(F)/wp_n W_n(F). There is a natural isomorphism Q_n(F)≃H¹(F,Z/p^nZ). For a class [a], adjoining a solution of wp_n(y)=a gives a cyclic extension of degree equal to the additive order of [a], not necessarily p^n. Two generator classes define the same subfield exactly when their generated cyclic subgroups of Q_n(F) agree.
hypotheses: p prime; CharP F p; Galois cohomology uses the constant Z/p^n module in the separable closure.
proofSteps: Descend native Frobenius through truncation; prove the ASW exact sequence over the separable closure and use additive Hilbert 90 successively through Witt truncations.
Identify a cyclic extension with its character subgroup. A chosen generator differs by a unit of Z/p^n, whereas a coboundary keeps the same character.

sources.match: Theorem 3.2 identifies ASW classes with continuous cyclic p-power characters using Witt Frobenius minus identity. Orders of classes determine extension degrees, and cyclic subgroups, rather than individual generators, determine the same cyclic field.

acceptance: The zero class gives F itself; full degree p^n requires a class of exact order p^n.

nodes.title: Reduced Witt Laurent data
nodes.statement: Let F=k((T)) with finite k of characteristic p, choose α∈k with nonzero trace to Fp and β=[α]∈W(k). Each class in Q_n(F) has a unique reduced expression cβ+Σ_{i>0,p∤i} c_i[T^(−i)], with c∈Z/p^nZ and c_i∈W_n(k); at fixed n only finitely many c_i are nonzero. Infinite compatible classes use c_i∈W(k) tending to zero p-adically. Reduction records the chosen parameter and β. At n≥1 its conductor exponent is 0 if all c_i vanish, otherwise 1+max_{c_i≠0} i p^(n−v_p(c_i)−1); v_p(c_i)<n for every nonzero truncated coefficient.
hypotheses: Finite residue field; chosen T and trace-nonzero β. Coefficients are Witt coefficients, not coordinatewise additive polynomials.
proofSteps: Eliminate pole orders divisible by p using wp and truncation; reduce the constant term via the trace quotient.
Prove uniqueness successively modulo p^j. Apply the ramification/upper-filtration calculation of Kosters–Wan Proposition 4.14; constants give the unramified part.

acceptance: The largest pole at a higher Witt valuation receives the smaller power of p in the conductor formula.

nodes.title: The one-pole Artin–Schreier test
nodes.statement: Over k(t), k finite of characteristic p, the cover y^p−y=t^(−m), m>0 and p∤m, is a geometrically connected cyclic degree-p cover. It is ramified only at t=0, with conductor m+1 and different exponent (p−1)(m+1); its genus is (p−1)(m−1)/2. At infinity the equation has residue y^p−y=0 and yields p rational places. This is the length-one ASW instance and imports the AC.7 different and Hurwitz theorem.
hypotheses: m positive and prime to p; RHS exactly t^(−m); k contains Fp.
proofSteps: The reduced pole shows the class is nonzero and cannot become constant, even after extending constants.
Apply the local conductor/different formula and the imported separable Hurwitz equation; inspect the unramified residue equation at infinity.

nodes.title: Equal-characteristic Lubin–Tate construction
nodes.statement: For a complete discretely valued field F of characteristic p with residue F_Q, uniformizer π, and valuation ring O, choose f(X)=πX+X^Q. Construct the unique commutative native FormalGroup O with f an endomorphism and its O-action having prescribed linear coefficient. For every m≥1 its π^m-torsion splitting field F_m/F is totally ramified abelian of degree (Q−1)Q^(m−1), with Galois action (O/π^m)×. The corresponding relative construction over finite unramified extensions permits a chosen x∈F× of positive valuation to replace π in the norm specification.
hypotheses: Complete discretely valued equal-characteristic local field; finite residue field; torsion points evaluated only in maximal ideals of finite extensions.
proofSteps: Use Yoshida Lemma 3.4’s coefficient recursion to construct the group law and O-action; uniqueness gives associativity and commutativity.

Appendix II, Proposition 8.1 proves torsion-polynomial separability also in characteristic p. Proposition 4.4 proves degree, uniformizer and Galois action. Use the relative unramified Frobenius twist of §§3–4 for arbitrary x.

sources.locator: §§3.1–4.2, Lemma 3.4, Proposition 3.5, Corollary 3.7, Proposition 4.4, pp.415–421; Appendix II, Proposition 8.1, pp.436–437
sources.match: Yoshida’s formal-module construction and Proposition 4.4 apply to equal characteristic as well as mixed characteristic. Specializing to f=πX+X^Q yields torsion degree (Q−1)Q^(m−1), including the nontrivial wild higher levels.

acceptance: At m=1 the degree is Q−1, prime to p; the higher factors supply the missing p-primary tower.

nodes.title: Full equal-characteristic local existence
nodes.statement: For a complete discretely valued field F of characteristic p with finite residue field and every open finite-index subgroup H⊆F×, there is a unique finite abelian subextension E/F in a chosen separable closure with N_{E/F}(E×)=H; [E:F]=[F×:H]. This includes p-primary H. The CFT.6–CFT.7 finite Artin map becomes an isomorphism F×/H≃Gal(E/F), normalized so a uniformizer acts by arithmetic Frobenius on unramified extensions.

Use Corollary 5.16 and §§6.1–6.3 for norm compatibility and exhaustion of abelian extensions. Compare the inverse of Yoshida’s geometric normalization with CFT’s arithmetic normalization on finite unramified quotients.

nodes.title: Schmid–Witt symbol and local Artin comparison
nodes.statement: On F=k((T)) with k finite and n≥1, pair Q_n(F) with F× by the action of the arithmetic local Artin map on solutions of wp_n(y)=a. It equals the truncation modulo p^n of Tr_{W(k)/Z_p} Res(ã dlog b̃), using Kosters–Wan’s characteristic-zero lifts of reduced Witt Laurent data and unit factors. The pairing kills (F×)^(p^n) and induces a perfect continuous pairing of the discrete group Q_n(F) with F×/(F×)^(p^n), carrying the quotient of the local-field topology. At a fixed n it is not perfect against the whole pro-p completion: nonzero p^n multiples in its valuation coordinate annihilate every Q_n character. The compatible infinite-length symbol uses the inverse-limit Witt quotient and pro-p completion with the topologies specified in Kosters–Wan §4.1. For a finite subgroup of Q_n(F), the compositum of its ASW extensions has norm subgroup equal to the common annihilator. The symbol is compared after local existence, never used in a circular proof of it.
hypotheses: k is a finite field of characteristic p and n≥1; finite-length and inverse-limit pairings have distinct multiplicative domains and topologies.
Residue and dlog computed in the specified characteristic-zero lift ring; Witt trace, not ghost-coordinate division in characteristic p.
proofSteps: Import local Artin from the existing class formation and the full existence theorem just proved.

At fixed length use Theorem 3.4 and Remark 4.1 to descend to F×/(F×)^(p^n). Check Theorem 4.7’s lifted-residue formula on a constant, a Teichmüller pole, a uniformizer and a principal unit; use bilinearity and the reduced expansion. Apply the norm-kernel theorem on each finite ASW layer and intersection under composita.

sources.locator: Theorem 3.4, p.8; §4.1, Remark 4.1, pp.14–15; Proposition 4.2, p.15; §4.4, Theorem 4.7 and proof, pp.18–19
sources.match: Theorem 3.4 and Remark 4.1 give the finite-length pairing with F×/(F×)^(p^n). Theorem 4.7 supplies the characteristic-zero lifted-residue formula. The infinite pro-p completion belongs to the compatible infinite-length symbol, not a perfect pairing with one fixed Q_n.

acceptance: Constant classes pair with the valuation of b and are trivial on units.
A reduced pole gives the conductor in FA.3; naive characteristic-p ghost division is excluded.
At n=1 a uniformizer raised to p pairs trivially with every class but has nonzero valuation coordinate p in the pro-p completion; perfectness requires the pth-power quotient.

nodes.title: The global function-field class formation
nodes.statement: For finite exact k and K=k(X), specialize the imported Tate class-formation machinery to the projective idele class modules of finite separable extensions. Local Brauer invariants and the global exact sequence Br(K)→⊕_v Br(K_v)→Q/Z give the invariant and fundamental classes. The Jacobian obstruction H¹(k,Jac_X) is zero by Lang over finite constants, including after every finite constant extension. Thus the global function-field idele formation has the Tate H¹-vanishing and normalized H² invariants required by CFT.1–CFT.4.
hypotheses: All completions are nonarchimedean; finite exact constants; no number-field archimedean terms. Tsen is SF.2/tsen-theorem, Lang’s theorem for the Jacobian is ReductiveGroupsPartII:RG2.3/lang-theorem, and the Picard–Brauer input is SF.3/picard-brauer-sequence.
proofSteps: Follow Milne ADT A.7: apply Tsen over algebraically closed constants and the divisor–Picard exact sequences, obtaining the global Brauer invariant sequence.

Use A.8–A.9 and Lang to kill the finite-field Jacobian obstruction, then feed this arithmetic formation into the generic Tate theorem of CFT.2–CFT.4. Existence is a separate arithmetic target and is not a class-formation axiom.

sources.locator: Appendix A, A.7–A.9 with proofs, pp.131–134
sources.match: Milne proves the finite-function-field class formation in A.7–A.9 using Picard, Lang and Tsen inputs. Tsen and Lang are cited from SF.2/tsen-theorem and RG2.3/lang-theorem and the Picard inputs from SF.3; no abelian existence theorem is used to establish the formation.

acceptance: The sum of local invariants of a global Brauer class is zero.
The formation theorem does not claim existence of class fields.

nodes.title: Global arithmetic Artin and the finite norm quotient
nodes.statement: For finite abelian L/K, the product of local arithmetic Artin maps defines a continuous surjective homomorphism I_K→Gal(L/K), is trivial on K×, and induces C_K/N_{L/K}C_L≃Gal(L/K). Local unramified units contribute trivially, so products in each finite quotient are finite. In a constant extension F_{q^r}K/K the image is arithmetic Frobenius to the power deg_val(a), equivalently to the power −deg_Yu(a). Norms, inclusions of fields and restriction of Galois actions satisfy the imported reciprocity diagram.
hypotheses: Finite abelian and separable extension in a fixed separable closure; no infinite product in an unspecified topology.
proofSteps: Use ADT A.10’s principal reciprocity law via the invariant sum and A.11’s formation Artin isomorphism.
Compare the local and formation maps on unramified uniformizers, then apply CFT.3–CFT.4 norm functoriality and norm limitation.

sources.match: A.10–A.11 derive finite norm quotients and reciprocity from the formation. The packet retains the abelian-extension hypothesis and separates this norm theorem from geometric existence.

acceptance: A principal idele maps to the identity.
A uniformizer at degree d acts on constant extensions as Frobenius^d.

nodes.title: Schmidt’s degree-one divisor theorem
nodes.statement: For a smooth projective geometrically connected curve X/Fq, gcd{deg v : v a closed point}=1. Hence an integer divisor of degree one exists, and the valuation degree C_K→Z is surjective. No degree-one closed point or rational point is asserted. This follows, independently of class field theory and of zeta rationality, from the curve Weil estimate EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.7/weight-weil-estimate-for-curves over every F_{q^r}, whose proof goes through the Jacobian.
hypotheses: Independent curve Weil bound |#X(Fq^r)−(q^r+1)|≤2g q^(r/2) for every r≥1, as stated in EDC.7/weight-weil-estimate-for-curves.
proofSteps: If h>1 divided all closed-point degrees, then X(Fq^r) would be empty whenever h∤r. Choose arbitrarily large such r; the Weil lower bound is eventually positive, a contradiction.
The gcd of a set of positive integers is the gcd of a finite subset. Bézout produces an integer divisor of degree one; the idele-divisor surjection supplies a degree-one idele.

sources.locator: §4.3.3, pp.25–28 (Schmidt context; the theorem is named on p.26); EDC.7/weight-weil-estimate-for-curves supplies the independent all-extension Weil estimate
sources.match: Roquette supplies historical context for Schmidt, not the proof adopted here. The independent all-extension Weil estimate forces closed-point degree gcd one; a Bezout combination gives a degree-one divisor, without requiring a rational point or FA.4 existence.

acceptance: A curve without Fq-points still admits an integer divisor of degree one.
No FA.4 theorem is a prerequisite of this node.

nodes.title: Ray subgroups and generalized Picard torsors
nodes.statement: For an effective modulus m=Σ_v m_v[v], define U_m⊆I_K by O_v× for m_v=0 and 1+𝔭_v^{m_v} for m_v>0. Put C_m=C_K/im U_m and C_m⁰=ker deg_val; C_m⁰ is finite and identifies with the k-points of the generalized Jacobian J_m, while degree gives 0→C_m⁰→C_m→Z→0. Pic_m¹ is a torsor; selecting Schmidt’s degree-one divisor gives an origin in the ray Picard torsor, not a rational point of X. C_m itself is infinite. A finite ray quotient additionally fixes a finite-index subgroup in the degree direction.
hypotheses: Finite exact constants; projective ray data including local trivialization at the modulus; residue at m=0 uses the ordinary Jacobian.
proofSteps: Use the divisor map away from m and weak approximation to compare ideles with line bundles trivialized along m.
Import generalized Picard representability/descent from SF.3. Use the finite constant-field points and Schmidt to split the degree sequence after a choice.

Pulling its torsor to X minus supp(m) along the ray Abel map gives the geometric ray cover. Constant extensions provide finite degree quotients. A suitable compositum has norm subgroup contained in H; its fixed subfield associated to H has exactly that norm subgroup by the already proved finite Artin isomorphism.

nodes.title: Profinite global reciprocity and constants
nodes.statement: The compatible finite Artin maps give a continuous dense-image map C_K→Gal(K^ab/K), and global existence induces an isomorphism of profinite completions Ĉ_K≃Gal(K^ab/K). Restriction to the constant algebraic closure is the completion of deg_val:C_K→Z, followed by n↦Frob_q^n. With a selected degree-one class, C_K≃C_K⁰×Z topologically and Ĉ_K≃C_K⁰×Ẑ. The uncompleted degree direction Z is not replaced by Ẑ without completion.

The modulus √q of the inverse roots is imported from EtaleDualityAndPerverseSheaves:EDC.7/weight-weil-estimate-for-curves, which also identifies P_X with the reversed characteristic polynomial of the Jacobian Frobenius; it is not obtained from rationality alone. nodes.title: Artin inertia factors with finite coefficients
nodes.statement: For a continuous finite-image representation ρ of Gal(K^sep/K) on a finite-dimensional vector space V over a field A of characteristic ℓ≠p, choose inertia I_v and geometric Frobenius Fr_v on V^{I_v}. The local factor polynomial is det(1−T^{d_v}ρ(Fr_v)|V^{I_v}); the local L-factor is its inverse. Frobenius is well-defined on inertia invariants and the determinant is independent of the lift and basis. Use the invariant subspace even if ℓ divides the inertia image order: averaging by #I_v is then invalid. A symplectic specialization additionally assumes ℓ≠2.

proofSteps: Import decomposition/inertia and finite-dimensional linear algebra. Restrict the chosen Frobenius lift to inertia invariants and substitute T^{d_v} in its characteristic determinant.
Lift independence follows because two lifts differ by inertia; basis independence follows by conjugacy.

nodes.title: Degree-sensitive finite Chebotarev, imported from DWP.3

Let M/K be finite Galois with group G, F_{q^h} the exact constants of M, N=Gal(M/F_{q^h}K), so |G|=h|N|, and for a conjugacy class C⊆G let π_C(r) count the unramified closed places of K of degree r with arithmetic Frobenius in C. If C does not map to Frob_q^r on F_{q^h}, then π_C(r)=0; otherwise |rπ_C(r)−(|C|/|N|)(q^r+1)|≤(2g_M+r(1+2g_X))q^{r/2}+r+R, where g_M is the genus of M over its exact constants and R the total degree of the ramified places of X. nodes.title: Cuspidal constant terms
nodes.statement: For each proper K-parabolic P=MN, N(K)∖N(A_K) is compact. Normalize its measure to total mass one. The cusp module is the intersection of all kernels CT_P. For complex coefficients this equals the ordinary normalized integral. Its level double-coset set is finite, so the cusp space is finite-dimensional over C. For split reductive G, compactness holds after bounding every rational-character degree, or after quotienting a full central degree lattice compatible with the character. Extension to arbitrary connected reductive G requires the nonsplit reduction theorem identified in request RG-RED; a GL₁ counterexample prevents asserting finiteness without the central restriction.

nodes.title: Whittaker comparison with imported Hermitian densities
nodes.statement: At an unramified quadratic local algebra F′_v/F_v, inert or split, import the integral Hermitian lattice L and normalized Siegel polynomial Den_v(X,L) from GN.2–GN.3. For the integral nonsingular Gram form T of L and FYZ’s section and additive character, W_{T,v}(1,s)=L_{n,v}(s)⁻¹ Den_v(q_v^(−2s),L), where L_{n,v}(s)=∏_{i=1}^n(1−η_v(π_v)^i q_v^(−i−2s))⁻¹. Its interpolation at nonnegative integers j uses the density ratio for source rank n+2j, hence X=q_v^(−2j), not the rank-n+j value with an unchanged argument. Integral-lattice generic nondegeneracy is distinct from self-duality.
hypotheses: p≠2 in the global application; F′_v unramified quadratic étale. The inert polynomial is already owned; the split extension is explicitly requested from GN.3.

nodes.title: FYZ regular global coefficient formula
nodes.statement: Let E be a rank-n vector bundle on X′ and a:E→σ*E∨ an injective Hermitian map, with E∨=Hom(E,ω_X′), the Serre dual. Define Den(X,(E,a))=∏_{v∈|X|}Den_v(X^{d_v},(E_v,a_v)); all but finitely many factors are 1. The regular Fourier coefficient of the normalized spherical Eisenstein series is χ(det E) q^{−deg E(s−n/2)−n²degω_X/2} L_n(s)⁻¹ Den(q^(−2s),(E,a)), where L_n=∏_v L_{n,v}. The formula is independent of the rational trivialization of E and of the canonical-line trivialization. It uses the Serre dual degree n degω_X′−deg E, not the ordinary dual degree −deg E.
hypotheses: Étale double cover of an odd-characteristic finite-field curve; χ and section normalized as above; a generically nonsingular/injective; vector-bundle and Hermitian lattice comparisons imported.

nodes.statement: For a verified separating presentation K/k(t) and its normalized finite/infinite integral bases, a place certificate is a maximal ideal in one chart, its verified finite residue-field encoding, normalized valuation and ramification/residue degrees. Divisor arithmetic uses the resulting native place-indexed finitely supported integer functions; a singular affine point can have several normalized places and is never accepted without normalization data.

nodes.title: L-polynomial certificates
nodes.statement: For a genus-g curve over Fq, an L-polynomial certificate contains certified counts N_r=#X(Fq^r) for 1≤r≤g, consumed from FF.3, and P∈Z[T]. Set a_0=1, s_r=q^r+1−N_r and recursively r a_r=−Σ_{i=1}^r s_i a_{r−i} for 1≤r≤g, checking exact divisibility. Fill a_{2g−r}=q^{g−r}a_r by FA.5’s functional equation. The verified polynomial equals P_X. For g=0 no count is needed and P=1. A list of unchecked counts or a mere Weil-shaped polynomial is not a certificate.
hypotheses: Curve and genus independently certified; each count certificate covers all projective points over its stated field. FF.3 currently supplies only an elliptic special case: request the general curve/hyperelliptic extension explicitly.

nodes.title: Ray-character and conductor certificates
nodes.statement: A finite ray-character certificate specifies a modulus m, a chosen finite degree quotient of C_m, its verified finite abelian-group presentation, a character into specified roots of unity, and local restrictions. Wild cyclic p-parts are verified using ReducedWittData and the Artin symbol; prime-to-p parts use imported tame reciprocity. The value on the selected degree-one class separately records the constant-field character.

nodes.title: Cost model and four end-to-end examples
nodes.statement: Fix a finite-field encoding by a monic irreducible polynomial over Fp, count both field operations and integer bit operations, and bound presentation degrees, coefficient bit lengths, divisor height h(D)=Σ|D_v|d_v and requested precision. RR reduction is polynomial in the verified matrix size/degrees and h(D), with normalization and factorization costs stated separately; a brute-force point count costs at least its enumerated q^r field elements, so no polynomial-in-log(q) claim is made. The examples are Fq(t); y²=x³+x+1 over F5 (smooth genus one, N_1=9, P=1+3T+5T²); its F25 constant extension (N_2=27, P=1+T+25T²); and y³−y=t⁻² over F3 (genus one, conductor 3[0], different 6[0], N_1=4, P=1+3T²). Parshin describes the discrete diagonal and compact adelic quotient, together with divisor lattices. The packet obtains these arithmetic comparisons from local approximation and imported Riemann–Roch, rather than identifying completed adeles with repartitions.

Parshin uses local differential residues and their global sum. AC.9 supplies parameter independence and the residue theorem; FA.2 extends to completed places and takes the residue-field trace to the exact constants.

The residue character is Parshin’s adelic pairing with the two corrections E1–E2: multiply local character values and use a nontrivial trace character. Finite-field trace pairing proves nondegeneracy without requiring an injective scalar character.

Parshin fixes differential-dependent self-dual local measures and gives the global integral-lattice volume. The packet derives q^(deg D+1−g) from local conductor exponents and the native canonical divisor degree, keeping local and global changes of differential distinct. Corrected the suggested signatures to require finite constants.

Parshin states adelic Fourier inversion and Poisson summation. The proof here corrects E3 by spanning the test space with translated compact-open indicators and uses the diagonal annihilator and quotient-volume normalization.

Kosters–Wan uses ramification and conductors of finite ASW extensions. General different, separability, Hurwitz and upper/lower numbering are existing AC/LFR inputs; this node records their use rather than planning their general theory again.

Theorem 3.2 identifies ASW classes with continuous cyclic p-power characters using Witt Frobenius minus identity. Orders of classes determine extension degrees, and cyclic subgroups, rather than individual generators, determine the same cyclic field.

Proposition 4.3 gives the reduced constant-plus-prime-to-p-pole form, with p-adically vanishing coefficients. Proposition 4.14 computes finite-layer conductors; truncation leaves only finitely many effective coefficients.

The length-one specialization of Proposition 4.14 gives conductor m+1 for the single prime-to-p pole. Imported ramification and Hurwitz then give different exponent (p−1)(m+1) and genus (p−1)(m−1)/2; the source is not claimed to enumerate the global curve.

Yoshida’s formal-module construction and Proposition 4.4 apply to equal characteristic as well as mixed characteristic. Specializing to f=πX+X^Q yields torsion degree (Q−1)Q^(m−1), including the nontrivial wild higher levels.

Yoshida computes relative Lubin–Tate norm subgroups and proves the open finite-index existence theorem, then identifies all finite abelian extensions using Hasse–Arf. His geometric Frobenius convention is inverted to the packet’s arithmetic convention.

Theorem 3.4 and Remark 4.1 give the finite-length pairing with F×/(F×)^(p^n). Theorem 4.7 supplies the characteristic-zero lifted-residue formula. The infinite pro-p completion belongs to the compatible infinite-length symbol, not a perfect pairing with one fixed Q_n. Corrected the finite-length perfect-pairing domain and added the p^n-power annihilator regression.

Milne proves the finite-function-field class formation in A.7–A.9 using Picard, Lang and Tsen inputs. These are requested explicitly from SF.3; no abelian existence theorem is used to establish the formation.
A.10–A.11 derive finite norm quotients and reciprocity from the formation. The packet retains the abelian-extension hypothesis and separates this norm theorem from geometric existence.

Roquette supplies historical context for Schmidt, not the proof adopted here. The independent all-extension Weil estimate forces closed-point degree gcd one; a Bezout combination gives a degree-one divisor, without requiring a rational point or FA.4 existence.

Conrad defines generalized Jacobians for a modulus and states their class-field relation. The arithmetic idele/divisor comparison includes local units at depth zero and a separate infinite degree direction; the generalized Picard construction remains an SF.3 input.
Conrad states the exact ray-cover and classification theorems. The packet honestly records that this handout does not verify the full Rosenlicht/Lang-torsor proof; GEO-RAY remains a closure boundary.

Milne supplies the finite norm quotients; existence supplies their cofinality. Taking finite quotients yields profinite reciprocity, with degree completed from Z to Z-hat rather than a false isomorphism of the uncompleted idele class group.

Roquette discusses the effective-divisor Euler product and its relation to finite-extension point counts. The formal logarithmic/Newton identities here are the stated arithmetic deduction, with residue degrees retained. Corrected the zero-coefficient theorem and example to require finite constants and an explicit function-field proof.

Roquette explains rationality and the functional equation from Riemann–Roch. The packet imports the Weil inverse-root bound independently from WC.5 and does not claim that Riemann–Roch proves that bound.

Equation (3.1) uses geometric Frobenius acting on actual inertia invariants. This also applies to the stated finite coefficient field with ℓ≠p; no averaging projector is imposed when ℓ divides the finite monodromy order.

Equation (3.2) expresses the torsion Euler product through all cohomological determinants on the proper curve. The packet distinguishes j_* inertia stalks from j_! extension by zero and requests the coefficient-accurate trace formula. Read PR196 TraceFormula; corrected the supplier contract through EDC.8’s existing upstream import, added the characteristic-ℓ power-trace counterexample, and recorded TORSION-DETERMINANT.

Kosters proves finite-field twist counting with Weil error. The displayed degree-r prime-count bound is the packet’s deduction after constant-field compatibility, base change, ramified-point exclusion and removal of lower-degree divisors; it is not quoted as his theorem.

The proof of Theorem 5.3.3 uses Chebotarev density and Brauer–Nesbitt for determination by Frobenius. Only that step is imported; continuous characteristic-zero semisimplicity is retained, without claiming the source’s broader coefficient-object theorem here. Moved the generic Brauer–Nesbitt enhancement request from DWP.1 to the DWP.0 linear-algebra direction.

Yu fixes the global adelic quotient, levels and central character in the finite-function-field setting. Generic reductive points are imported; the packet bounds or quotients every central degree direction before making finiteness claims. Replaced the Mathlib convolution group citation by TauCeti.AlgHom.instGroup, which supports arbitrary commutative value algebras.

BHKT defines cuspidality by every proper rational parabolic and proves finite-level finiteness. The integral construction uses finite p-power averages with p invertible and common support; torus cuspidality alone does not remove its infinite degree direction.
Harder proves common support bounds and compactness for split Chevalley groups. The packet preserves this proved scope and explicitly conditions the nonsplit connected-reductive extension on RG2.4.

Ciubotaru–Harris proves fixed-level cusp finiteness and the complex scalar comparison over Noetherian coefficient subrings of C. Such an embedding is flat via the fraction field. Hecke eigenvalue algebraicity is restricted to arithmetic coefficient models, not arbitrary transcendental characters. Clarified that R→C is flat through Frac(R); the original comparison was valid.

BHKT’s integral unramified Hecke setup fixes the needed coefficients and Satake normalization. The generic local Hecke/Satake construction is imported from SR.4; FA.6 supplies the global fixed-level action. Removed the repeated SR.4 prerequisite.

Yu’s Lemma 5.3.3 and proof give spherical degree-zero nonvanishing through Whittaker reconstruction. The packet requires a nonzero vector and corrects the determinant-degree and scalar-power signs recorded in E4–E5.

FYZ Remark 2.1 gives the unramified character extension with the stated restriction to F×. Its modulo-two argument uses alternating cup product, requested through integral Z_2 cohomology rather than inferred from graded commutativity over F_2.

FYZ fixes the quasi-split skew-Hermitian unitary group, spherical section and unnormalized exponent s+n/2. Convergence and continuation are separately imported with explicit function-field enhancement requests to AS.1 and AS.2.

FYZ defines the residue character on the Hermitian unipotent, the global quotient measure and the local integral-volume-one Fourier coefficients. Their differential-dependent prefactor and Levi transformation law are retained without mixing the two measure conventions.

FYZ proves the unramified inert and split density polynomials and compares them with local Whittaker integrals. Existing GN.3 inert data are reused; split density and the source-rank n+2j Siegel–Weil normalization are explicit supplier enhancements.

FYZ’s Theorem 2.8 gives the regular injective Hermitian bundle coefficient, including the determinant character, degree exponent and Euler normalization. Serre duality uses the canonical line, and the packet retains weighted total degree for split or constant covers.

Hess uses finite-prime factorization and integral normalization to access places. FA.7’s new contract assembles native normalized branches, infinity and degree-bounded completeness; factorization remains imported from FF.3.

Roquette supplies zeta identities. The proof-bearing certificate is our Newton and functional-equation deduction from independently certified complete counts through genus g; Weil-shaped coefficients alone are insufficient.

Kosters–Wan computes the wild local conductor. Combining this with Conrad’s ray-class contract gives the proposed finite presentation certificate. Depth zero means O_v×, and the finite degree quotient and degree-one value are specified separately. Corrected the depth-zero unit group, added finite image to the Lean certificate, and changed its degree-one condition to Yu degree −1.

Parshin identifies local curve fields as Laurent series. Yoshida explains uniformizer expansions in a complete DVR; together with the AC.5 coefficient-field and completion interfaces these justify the normalized local certificate, not an identification of the global field with its completion. Added an actual valuation-preservation proof field to the Lean certificate.

Hess separates integral-basis, factorization and degree/height reduction costs. The global ASW example’s local conductor comes from Kosters–Wan. Exhaustive extension-field point counts are finite verification tasks, not a polynomial-in-log(q) counting claim.
